brief.prompt: Q3 2026 investor update for Harbor, a freight-booking marketplace.

pasted.title: Q3
pasted.text: Revenue $3.9M vs plan $4.4M. GMV $41M, up 18% QoQ. Take rate 9.5%. Gross margin 34% vs plan 37%. Shipper retention 88%. Missed plan because two enterprise deals slipped to Q4. Burn $640k/month, cash $5.1M, 8 months runway. Hired a VP Sales in August. Asking for a $3M bridge.

brief.ask: Get approval for the bridge round and two intros to enterprise shippers

questions.question: Which KPIs should anchor the Q3 2026 update for your investors and board?
suggestions: Gross bookings, take rate, and repeat shipper rate
Carrier supply, shipper activation, and booking conversion

questions.question: What is the one sentence they must remember after this update?
suggestions: Harbor's Q3 momentum is real, and a bridge gets us to enterprise shippers.
Marketplace liquidity is improving; the bridge buys time to land anchor accounts.
We're capital-efficient, and two intros turn our pilots into enterprise revenue.

questions.question: What proof do you have for Q3 (traction, revenue, customers, pilots, quotes)?
suggestions: Q3 KPI dashboard and shipper pilot results, which I'll paste

questions.question: How many minutes do you have, and are you presenting live or sending it?
suggestions: 10 minutes, presented live at the board meeting
20 minutes live, leaving time for discussion
Sent ahead as a read-only deck before the meeting

outline.governing_thought: Harbor's marketplace is growing and keeping shippers; a $3M bridge carries it through two delayed enterprise deals and closes the revenue gap.
outline.ask: Get approval for the bridge round and two intros to enterprise shippers
key_points: Revenue $3.9M and gross margin 34% both missed plan
Two enterprise deals slipped to Q4
Cash of $5.1M gives 8 months of runway
Ask: approve the $3M bridge and make two enterprise shipper intros

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Harbor grew freight volume 18% in Q3 but missed plan

slides.notes: Thanks everyone for making time. We'll give you the Q3 picture in one line: the marketplace grew, with freight volume up 18%, but we missed our revenue plan. We'll show you what drove each part of that, why we think the miss is about timing rather than demand, and what we need from this board to bridge it. We'll keep it short and leave most of the time for your questions on the ask at the end.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Shippers booked $41M of freight on Harbor this quarter

fields.name: stat-label
fields.text: Q3 gross merchandise value, up 18% quarter over quarter

slides.notes: Start with the part that went right. Shippers booked $41 million of freight through Harbor this quarter, and that is up 18% on Q2. That number is gross merchandise value, the total freight moved on the platform, so it is the best read we have on whether shippers want to use us. Revenue is a share of that volume, and that is where the quarter got harder. Let's turn to how we did against the plan we set.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Revenue and gross margin both landed below plan

slides.notes: Here is the miss, plainly. Revenue came in at $3.9 million against a $4.4 million plan, so we are $500 thousand short. Gross margin was 34% against a 37% plan, three points light. We are not going to dress either number up. The next two slides separate what is working from what caused the gap, because the volume growth you just saw tells us the shortfall is not coming from the core marketplace.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Shippers stay: 88% retention and a 9.5% take rate

slides.notes: Before the cause of the miss, here is what held. Shipper retention reached 88%, so the shippers we win keep booking with us. Our take rate held at 9.5%, which means we are not buying volume by cutting price. And we hired a VP of Sales in August, which matters because the gap we are about to describe sits in enterprise sales. Those three facts are why we read this quarter as a timing problem and not a demand problem.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Two enterprise deals slipped to Q4 and caused the revenue miss

fields.name: point-1
fields.text: The shortfall is timing, not lost demand

fields.name: point-2
fields.text: Both deals now fall in Q4

slides.notes: The cause is two enterprise deals that slipped out of Q3 and into Q4. That is what produced the revenue miss. The important point is that this is timing, not lost demand. Neither shipper walked away, and both deals now fall in Q4. We would rather be direct that the slip was ours to forecast better, and our new VP of Sales is now working both of these deals. Next, what this means for cash.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Current cash funds eight more months of operations

fields.name: stat-label
fields.text: runway at the current $640k monthly burn

slides.notes: Here is the cash position. We have $5.1 million in the bank and we are burning $640 thousand a month. At that rate we have eight months of runway. That is workable but not comfortable, especially when the revenue we planned for Q3 has moved into Q4. A thin runway while two deals are still closing is exactly the situation a bridge is designed to cover, which brings us to the request.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: A $3M bridge covers the gap while enterprise deals close

fields.name: stat-label
fields.text: bridge round requested from existing investors

slides.notes: We are asking our existing investors for a $3 million bridge round. The purpose is narrow: it covers the gap while the two enterprise deals close, so we are not forced to make cuts or a rushed raise from a weak position. The marketplace is growing and shippers are staying, so this money is carrying a business that is already working through a timing delay. Let us be specific about what we need from you today.

fields.name: headline
fields.text: Approve the $3M bridge and introduce us to two enterprise shippers

fields.name: point-1
fields.text: Board approval of the $3M bridge round

slides.notes: Two things. First, we ask the board to approve the $3 million bridge round. Second, we ask for two introductions to enterprise shippers. Intros matter because enterprise deal timing is what hurt us this quarter, and a wider set of enterprise conversations reduces our dependence on any single deal closing on schedule. We are happy to take questions now, and we can go deeper on any number you have seen.
